No. The story is a quiet, atmospheric slice-of-life piece about a ferry crossing in fog. It is coherent and consistent, but it has no real turns that subvert expectations.

The closest thing to a turn is the late phone call from her son Jonas. It reveals that a sale of the ferry rights is pending and that he is pushing her to give up her house. This adds subtext, but it arrives as quiet exposition rather than a surprising development.

Ilse's response, ignoring the call and focusing on docking, fits her terse, stoic character, so it is appropriate. It is also exactly what the reader expects from her, so it is not surprising.

The story favours mood and restraint over unpredictability, so it does not achieve the balance of surprise and appropriateness.
